turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come through, love. You look a bit worn out. What's brought you in today?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Didn't want to come, if I'm honest. I'm tired, and it's these morning sweats and the shakes. That's the whole reason.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sounds miserable. Walk me through what a morning's like.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): I wake up dripping. Hands shaking. Err, three weeks of it now. I feel rotten until I eat, if I even eat.
[SEG0005] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She doesn't eat, doctor. Mum's been skipping brekky most days.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh leave it. I'm not hungry at six. The trains were stuffed again, but that's not... anyway.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right. So the sweating and the shaking are on you before any food. How often is that?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Pretty much every morning. Some days worse. I'm over it.
[SEG0009] person_3 (CAREGIVER): And one morning last week she was confused. Couldn't sort the kettle, kept asking me what day it was.
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): I was not confused. I was half asleep. Well, actually, that once I wasn't making sense. It passed after a cup of tea.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Okay. Settled after the tea. Any chest pain when this happens?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No chest pain. Don't add things.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Fair enough. What about your breathing? Any cough, or getting short of breath?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Breathing's fine.
[SEG0015] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She is wiped by lunch though. Flat on our couch. She moved in with us last year, so I see all of it.
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah I'm knackered. Couch is lumpy, write that down if you like.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ha, lumpy couch. The diabetes has been with you a good while though, hasn't it. How long?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Fifteen-odd years. Umm. Tablets, not the needles. Thank goodness.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): What tablets, and what doses are you on these days?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No idea. The chemist does a Webster pack. Metforman and the other one. Ask her, I'm sick of the questions.
[SEG0021] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Gliclazide, eighty milligrams, every morning. Metformin, five hundred milligrams, morning and night. She does take them.
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): And that gliclazide still goes down on the mornings with no brekky?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Yep. Swallow it with water, down the hatch. Food can wait.

[SEG0024] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Sorry, side note. My husband left his metformin in the car boot again. His are the one gram tablets, not Mum's. And he reckons Aunty Pam's biotin is why her nails grew. Rubbish.
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): Pam can keep the biotin. I'm not taking that.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll leave both of those alone. Any reactions to medicines? Anything you're allergic to?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Penicillin. I get a red rash all over and my lips swell up. Years ago. They told me never to have it again.
[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): Penicillin, rash and swollen lips. We'll steer well clear of that. Mind if I check you over?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): If you must. Be quick, I want a lie down.

[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): Pulse is seventy-six, nice and regular. Blood pressure's one forty-two over seventy-eight. Hands are cool and a bit clammy. Chest is clear, heart sounds normal, and the tummy's soft with nothing tender.
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm. Cold hands. Story of my life.
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): I reckon these morning sweats and shakes are low sugars, hypos, from the gliclazide on an empty stomach. That muddled morning fits the same thing.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): So I'm not losing the plot. Good. I suppose.
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not losing the plot. I do want bloods today, the HbA1c and a kidney check while you're on metformin. We'll book both.
[SEG0035] person_3 (CAREGIVER): The pathology on High Street, same as usual?

[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yeah, reception out the front will book it. Have some brekky with that gliclazide, even toast. If you get shaky, juice or a few jelly beans and sit yourself down. Come back and see me in two weeks with the results, I'm not changing the dose today.
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Two weeks. Toast. Fine. I'm done in.

spec.situation: Older diabetic on gliclazide and metformin with morning sweating and shakiness; skips breakfast; daughter reports confusion once; doctor reviews doses and plans a blood test.

traps.happens: The doctor asks about drug reactions. Variants (use ONE per encounter): (a) the patient says 'No, never, I have taken penicillin and everything' (no allergy); (b) the patient is unsure ('maybe the antibiotic or the painkiller, nobody told me which'); (c) a real allergy with the reaction described; (d) allergies are never asked.
traps.label_rule: (a) NO allergy entry: negative_findings 'Allergies' absent. (b) allergy with status uncertain, the substance as described, the reaction if said, plus an allergy_uncertain uncertainty. (c) allergy with the reaction. (d) nothing at all. NEVER list a medicine the patient has taken without a reaction as an allergy, and the plan must not prescribe a drug of a recorded allergy's family.

features: spoken_numbers: doses, vitals and durations are spoken as words or sloppy speech ('a hundred and two point five', 'one-forty over ninety', 'five-ish years', 'twenty milligram'); the label writes them normally (102.5, 140/90, 20 mg) and does not turn vague ones into exact ones.

third_party_medicine: someone mentions a medicine or condition that belongs to a relative or friend (the sister's biotin, the husband's metformin). It must not appear as the patient's own; a relative's illness can only be family history if said as such.
